title: The Coaching Trap: Why Better Teaching Depends on Better Schools
author: David Didau
summary: David Didau critiques instructional coaching as a school improvement strategy, arguing that while coaching has real evidence behind it (Kraft et al's meta-analysis of 60 studies found positive effects on both instructional practice and student achievement), those effects shrink dramatically as programs scale. The root problem, Didau argues, is that schools take the structural form of coaching—the cycles, coaches, target-setting, forms—and assume they've captured the thing itself, when they've actually built monitoring with a thin veneer of support. Effective coaching, he insists, is a relationship organized around expertise: remove the expertise and you have therapy; remove the relationship and you have surveillance. More fundamentally, coaching is limited by the school environment it operates in. A teacher can be coached to improve questioning technique, but an unreliable behavior system blunts that improvement. Research shows teachers in schools at the 75th percentile for professional environment ratings improve 38% more over ten years than those at the 25th percentile—a larger effect than coaching alone. Didau concludes that school improvement must shift from an individualistic model (fix teachers one at a time) to a systemic one (build the conditions in which teachers improve naturally), and that this requires leaders who prioritize order, purposeful collaboration, instructionally credible leadership, high trust, and coherent culture.
points: Coaching effects degrade at scale because the conditions that make coaching work—expert coaches, precise feedback, protected time, close monitoring—cannot be guaranteed system-wide, so schools end up doing coaching's visible structure without its substance.

Effective coaching is a relationship organized around expertise: without the expertise it becomes therapy; without the relationship it becomes monitoring—and most school coaching programs mistake one of these lesser things for the real article.

Teacher improvement is environmentally determined: teachers in high-quality professional environments improve 38% more over ten years than those in low-quality ones, which means the return on improving the school system exceeds the return on coaching any individual teacher within it.

A teacher can be coached on technique, but behavior systems, curriculum coherence, assessment infrastructure, and trust are outside individual teacher control—and coaching leaves those untouched, which is why coaching in dysfunctional schools rarely holds.

School improvement thinking is 'too individualistic': weak teaching is treated as the property of weak teachers, when it is often the product of weak schools—and building the conditions for improvement (order, purposeful collaboration, high trust, coherent culture, instructionally credible leadership) is the real job of leadership.
quotes: Most professional development is barely professional development at all. Teachers are gathered in a hall, shown a few slides, invited to discuss something agreeably vague about pedagogy, and then released back into classrooms where nothing much has changed.

Installing air conditioning is likely to do more for student outcomes than business-as-usual CPD. That sounds far fetched only if we assume the main barriers to better teaching are always located inside teachers. Often they're in the fabric of the school itself.

Coaching isn't a mechanism, or a product that can be bought off the shelf. For it to be effective, instructional coaching is relationship organised around expertise. If the expertise is removed it becomes little more than therapy. And if the relationship is removed, it becomes monitoring.

Teachers improve at different rates depending on the professional environments in which they work. Teachers in schools at the 75th percentile for professional environment ratings improved 38% more over ten years than teachers in schools at the 25th percentile.

Schools routinely try to improve one teacher at a time while leaving the system that shapes their work largely untouched. Why? Because it's far easier to blame inadequate teachers than to recognise you've created the conditions in which inadequacy flourishes.
If we want better teachers we need better schools. And if we want better schools, we need better school leaders.

A teacher can be coached to improve their questioning, but an unreliable behaviour system will still blunt the effect; they can learn to model more clearly, but an incoherent curriculum leaves the model directionless.
